stories.headline: Real Madrid best Barça in brilliant Clásico; Man United mess deepens; Spurs win again
stories.summary: The weekend's big games brought plenty to unpack, with Real Madrid's Clásico win slowing Barcelona down in LaLiga and Man United's heavy home defeat surely pushing Michael Carrick toward the exit.
stories.body:
What a weekend in European football! The Clásico in LaLiga well and truly delivered on the hype, with Jose Mourinho and Real Madrid walking away impressive 2-1 winners over Barcelona in front of a stunned Camp Nou crowd. In the big Premier League clash, Tottenham broke a historic winless streak to win 2-0 at Chelsea, while Man United's malaise deepened with a 3-0 home defeat against Bournemouth, one that might well spell the end of the Michael Carrick era at Old Trafford.

Elsewhere, we have talking points galore around Arsenal, Inter Milan, Bayern Munich, Liverpool, Borussia Dortmund and much more.

It's Monday morning, so what better time for some musings? Let's get into it.

- Dawson: Man United are stuck no matter who's boss

- Reaction: Mourinho guides Real Madrid to statement win over Barcelona

- Lindop: Iraola era at Liverpool finally has liftoff thanks to Isak, Barcola

Real Madrid blow LaLiga wide open with Clásico win

Yes, I know it sounds unhinged to talk about "reopening" the title race a few days before Halloween, with some 28 games to go. But such was Barcelona's dominance -- statistical, emotional and perceived -- just a few days back that a Clásico win over Real Madrid would have had the effect of supergluing the coffin shut. It's not hard to game out that scenario.

With a victory, Barcelona would have pulled nine points clear at the top of LaLiga and equaled Real Madrid in the all-time head-to-head. Jose Mourinho would be finding something to complain about and the Florentino Perez War Machine would be amplifying it. His critics would be pointing out that three straight away games were next, followed by the international break, i.e. sacking season. Lamine Yamal would be crowing on Ballon d'Or Day, while Kylian Mbappé would be catching strays from the folks who like to talk about individual statistics versus team awards.

Except all of that belongs to an alternate -- if very plausible -- universe. In reality, Real Madrid's 2-1 win means they're just three points back. (And Atlético Madrid, who are two back, might well have the opportunity to leapfrog Barça when they host them on Nov. 8.)

Once again, Mourinho disrupted the script. And he did it not in the way we've seen him do it at times in years past -- turning the game into a gladiatorial arena, flipping out at the match officials, grinding things out by any means necessary -- but by "out-footballing" Barcelona in their own house.

Let's be clear: both teams could have scored more, and this game could have taken a very different turn. Yamal squandered an early chance, Gerard Martín could have been smarter with his clearance, Raphinha more accurate with his finishing. But equally, Jude Bellingham could have released a wide open Kylian Mbappe in the second half instead of taking it himself, Mbappe could have not shanked that first-half chance, and Real Madrid could have been more clinical too. If you're the sort of person who just parses football down to episodes and highlights, you can argue this any which way.

More telling is what we saw beyond the obvious flashpoints at the Camp Nou. Yamal was shut down by a combination of Marc Cucurella and Yan Diomande. Pedri and Rodri were more than matched in the middle of the park by the combination of Bernardo Silva, Aurélien Tchouaméni and, when he came inside, Arda Güler. Raphinha was forced to retreat to find service. On the day, Mourinho out-coached Hansi Flick.

The Madrid coach turned Vinícius Junior's suspension into a positive, letting Diomande roam on the left, where he does his best work. Bernardo Silva added quality, geometry (and, occasionally, the right bite) to midfield. Andriy Lunin, deputizing for Thibaut Courtois, had zero stage fright (and was rewarded with a big hug from his coach after the game). Fede Valverde might not be the permanent answer at right back that's been lying in plain sight for years, but in a game like this he was hugely effective in both phases of play. Bellingham, while not flawless, tormented Rodri and was at the heart of several goal-scoring opportunities, as well as the winner. Eduardo Camavinga and Denzel Dumfries were the right substitutions at the right time.

Flick didn't adjust to Real Madrid because he's of the school that adapting to your opponent, especially at home, is a sign of weakness. Fine. But at least in terms of personnel -- on a night when the World Cup winning tandem of Rodri and Pedri were struggling -- you would have expected him to act sooner.

Absentees were a legitimate mitigating factor for Barça. Already without two fullback options in Jules Koundé and Eric García, he lost another one after half an hour when Xavi Espart was forced off for Alejandro Balde. Going for the win late on is nice and all (and in line with his DNA), but it ended up exposing Barça and, with hindsight, felt like a needless gamble. In the beat-the-dead-horse department, their defending cost them, too -- not so much the high line, but it's execution. (Maybe that was somewhat predictable when your fullbacks consist of João Cancelo and Balde, who had played 30 minutes of football to that point.)

Perhaps the individual quality was lacking as well: Gerard Martin (also a recycled a fullback playing center back) mishitting the ball across the face of his own goal is hard to accept at this level. When Flick turned to the bench to bring on attacking reinforcements and found himself turning to Gabriel Jesus and Karim Adeyemi, you couldn't help but wonder about how the club allocated its limited -- but precious -- resources in the summer.

Clásicos are a chance to set (and reset) the narrative. Both clubs can come out of this stronger. Getting spanked by Paris Saint-Germain and losing at home to Real Madrid can help remind Barcelona that despite the four goals a game, the going is tougher against the other super clubs, foreign and domestic. And obviously for Mourinho and Real Madrid, it's a reminder that they're not just a star-laden psychodrama/soap opera: they have outstanding players who are willing to work for a coach who can still be outstanding. And there's everything yet to play for in LaLiga.

As Man United mess gets worse, it's far easier to replace a manager than an owner or a bunch of players...

And that's why Michael Carrick should go, following Sunday's 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth. The question to be asked isn't whether he deserves to be fired, it's whether we can realistically imagine a Manchester United competing at some point for league titles and Champions Leagues with him at the helm in the medium term. The answer in my view is "no."

It's not just the track record, nor the sense of drift that remains, nor the shambles in Como, not just the horror show against Bournemouth. It's the fact that this group doesn't seem to respond to him. That's a big part of the manager's job; whatever stratagems he has tried to come up with, they're not working and, in fact, smack of desperation.

If you're going to discipline your captain, Bruno Fernandes, for speaking out of turn in midweek, then do it: leave him out of the matchday squad entirely. Or if you must include him on the bench, like he did Sunday, make sure people know he's being punished. But when you tell folks that your best player (by a country mile) has been benched for "purely footballing reasons," you look silly. There is no "purely footballing reason" why Bruno shouldn't be starting. By saying that, you're implying that you understand nothing about football (and we know that's not the case) or that the decision was made above your head (which would be worrying).

However, if Carrick is removed, he can't be the fall guy. Everybody knows he is not the only issue at the club. The fans who applauded Carrick and booed the players get this. If director of football Jason Wilcox or CEO Omar Berrada or co-owner Jim Ratcliffe had done a lap of honor such as Carrick, they would have been booed too. This is a collective failure.

At this point, there are two likely outcomes: both of them are bad, but one less so than the other. The worse one is that Carrick gets bumped -- either now or in a couple weeks -- everybody stays in their job, the Glazers count down the hours until Ratcliffe leaves, some interim guy comes in, there's another coaching search and we're no further forward in 12 months' time. The least bad one is that you write off the season -- whether with Carrick at the helm or someone else -- and use the time to test your youngsters and assess what you have. At the same time, you start, top down, with yet another rebuild -- one that begins with Ratcliffe riding into the sunset, and the Glazers taking the time and resources to evaluate everything from Berrada on down.

Either way, it's going to be ugly and for United fans, it's going to feel like Groundhog Day.

Spurs' win at Stamford Bridge speaks volumes about what both sides want to do

It was only Tottenham Hotspur's second win in their past 35 attempts at Chelsea, and after their horrendous start to the Premier League season, two wins on the spin feels pretty good. We saw Spurs play the way Roberto De Zerbi wants them to play, and while Chelsea's abject performance had a lot to do with it, De Zerbi Ball is one of those weird phenomena that has a cumulative effect: The more they get to do it, the better at it they become and the better it works. That Spurs were able to do it on the road in a fixture that traditionally gets edgy and physical (as evidenced by Cole Palmer's red card) only makes it more meaningful.

The goals came late -- the first a gift from stand-in keeper Mike Penders -- but were ultimately deserved. I've hammered Mathys Tel for so long, I was positively elated to see his run and finish to put the game beyond doubt.

As for Chelsea, they confirmed the doubts many of us had in the summer. Plenty will focus on the fact that in João Pedro's absence, Xabi Alonso opted to play Morgan Rogers up front rather than a traditional striker like Danny Welbeck. But Welbeck is 35 -- and looked it when he started against Brentford -- and Alonso sees him every day, so I tend to give him the benefit of the doubt. (Emmanuel Emegha, Chelsea's other center forward, is injured again and a long-term project. He has hardly played, or scored, since the 2024-25 season.) That's down to squad construction.

To me, Chelsea's real issue is midfield. Giving Spurs so much of the ball (69%) at home is problematic to begin with because it plays to their strengths. It's also not the way a top club should be playing week in, week out. They have had the bulk of possession in less than half of their games this season. Again, you have to question squad construction: Chelsea are light in that area of the pitch, no matter how good Moisés Caicedo is. When your answer is four consecutive starts for 36-year-old Jordan Henderson, you either have a serious issue or you're asking the wrong question.

And a final word on Palmer, who was sent off with 10 minutes to go for a second yellow. Truth be told, he could well have gone for the first, when he barged into a prone Mateus Fernandes. The way he shouted, "What?! What?!" at the referee spoke to his evident frustration. You don't want to make too big a deal out of it -- Palmer rarely shows indiscipline -- but it wasn't a good look.

Quick hits

10. Last season's Arsenal show up in win over Everton: I don't mean it in a derogatory sense, but the fact both goals in the 2-0 win over the Toffees came from set pieces is too hard to ignore. Last year, they notched 36 in all competitions (25 of them in the Premier League) and set-piece guru Nicolas Jover became a household name. Saturday's goals were the first two they managed this campaign (the first was facilitated by some bad defending) after going the first 12 matches with a big goose egg. It's not to minimize the importance of set pieces, but yes, variance is very much a thing.

It's pretty evident that Mikel Arteta -- whether he admits it or not -- has been playing differently this season, possibly because arguably his three biggest attacking talents (Bukayo Saka, Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz) have been mostly fit and firing, unlike most of last year. Against Everton, with Saka injured, Ødegaard understated and Havertz on the bench until the final 20 minutes, they reverted to the 2025-26 edition. That's not a bad thing; in fact it's a very handy change of pace to have. But to go the next level (and stay there) Arsenal need to play more like this season's version.

9. Christian Pulisic fires resurgent AC Milan into third place: One of the side effects of the expanded group stages in European football is that there's often no common thread from one game to the next. It means Milan can get humiliated away to Bournemouth on Thursday and, three days later, make five changes and look brilliant away to Udinese. And no, it's not just that Bournemouth are better than Udinese and the fact that there were five new players, but it does help.

Pulisic played from the start, scored an early goal (with some delicious close control) and could have had a hat-trick of assists. Luka Modric, confirming the "less is more" concept, dispensed magic. It looked like they're starting to metabolise Ruben Amorim's system, and the manager continues to push younger players: Sankhoun Diawara, 20, made his debut and looked good, while five of the players who featured were 22 or younger. There are still injuries and Goncalo Ramos still looks like a foreign object, but the fact of the matter is Milan are still undefeated and are third with the same number of points of Roma, who have gotten tons of praise all season. That's not nothing.

8. Beier to the rescue as Borussia Dortmund stay top amidst some unfair criticism: It took a late wonder-strike from substitute Maxi Beier for Dortmund to down Eintracht Frankfurt at home and stay atop the Bundesliga. The goal came late, but I thought Nico Kovac's crew was largely in control throughout and, with some better finishing could have gone into the break a couple goals up.

Which is why I find some of the anger directed at Kovac a little unfair. Yes, sharing first place with Bayern Munich feels a little flukey now and yes, heading into Saturday they had won just one of four (and that was against -- ahem -- Sabah FK, when they squandered an industrial quantity of changes) and yes, they're not particularly exciting to watch. But the results are there, the injuries are a legitimate mitigating factor and at least we know there's another gear that can be reached. A bit of stability isn't a bad thing for this club.

7. Liverpool still not pretty, but that's four wins on the bounce: Not only are they not pretty, they're also not really giving off that Andoni Iraola vibe just yet, and as I wrote last week, they won't be giving it off for some time. But Sunday's 2-0 win over a red-hot Brighton was not something to be taken for granted, and it sees them rise up into fourth place. Results matter when you're a new boss still trying to instill your values.

You can turn your nose up at 36% possession at home, but that's a natural by-product of going two goals up early against a side like Brighton. You can point out that Florian Wirtz got lucky with his deflection and that while Alexander Isak is on a scoring tear, he's still nowhere near where he was when he was still at Newcastle. All true. But when you've got injuries and the games are coming thick and fast, a little bit of drive, work rate, humility and commitment go a long way. Ronald Araujo might have been playing to the crowd a little bit, but it plays nicely at Anfield and it shows a unity of purpose. Equally, Bradley Barcola hasn't yet offered anywhere near the attacking output to justify his transfer fee, but he ran himself into the ground defensively like the most humble of wingers on a promoted side, rather than a diva transferred in from the champions of Europe. If the goal is to build an Iraola team at Anfield, this is still a work in progress that will take a long time (and different personnel) to come to fruition. But in the meantime, it's nice to get the pressure of results out of the way...

6. Internazionale dig deep to regain top spot in injury time: As the clock struck 90 minutes, things were looking bleak for Inter away at Fiorentina. David de Gea had saved everything in sight and, when he didn't get to the ball, the woodwork did, denying Inter twice. (Inter's xG of 3.75 at the final whistle says it all.) Lazio had won the night before, Inter needed three points the catch them. Christian Chivu emptied his bench, including 19-year-old debutant center forward Matteo Lavelli. It worked. Marcus Thuram, perhaps feeling more responsibility with Lautaro Martínez out, conjured up a wickedly accurate de facto pass into the back of the net that eluded De Gea. He then drew the foul from Viery after a flick on from the kid Lavelli and Piotr Zielinski converted from the spot in the eighth minute of injury time.

Once again Inter turned it around: it's now 13 points that they've gained this season after falling behind. I'm not big on narrative, but not everybody feels that way. And if Chivu can sell them on this (corny, but effective) never-say-die schtick it may well become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

5. Julián Álvarez scores winner for Atlético Madrid and says sorry ... two months too late: I guess we'll find out whether Álvarez's apology has traction with the fans. Doubtless the relationship will never be the same, but the best-case scenario is he sticks around for a while because he and the club have common goals: winning games. After all, we don't necessarily love our plumber (and he doesn't love us): we just want him to unblock our toilet, and he just wants to get paid. And Álvarez did unblock the toilet (metaphorically) scoring the only goal in Atleti's 1-0 home win over Deportivo. Amazingly it was his first home league goal from open play in nearly 13 months: making you wonder if maybe the club wouldn't actually have been better off without him and with a big wad of cash in his place.

Referring to his attempt to engineer a move to Barcelona in the summer, Álvarez said it was a "mistake" in terms of "how I said it and the timing." Not that he's learned much in terms of timing, because waiting two months to say sorry (or, really, say anything) is also a mistake. Unless he figured that doing it after scoring a game winner might make fans more accepting. (News flash: Real fans aren't that gullible.) As for the game itself, it's six wins on the spin in LaLiga, but this was not a great performance and you can see Atleti's participation in the UEFA Champions League taking its toll. Without Kevin Sánchez's miss-of-the-season contender in injury time, this would (and should) have been two points dropped.

4. Bayern Munich play with fire, but ultimately beat down SC Freiburg ambitions: Bayern are simply so much more talented than just about anyone else they face in the Bundesliga that often you feel that if they drop points, it's because they've beaten themselves. There were shades of that away to Freiburg on Sunday. They took the lead (on an improbable Dayot Upamecano counterattack that saw the big man rumble through the length of the pitch), doubled it in the second half and squandered plenty chances to put the game to bed. Eight minutes from time, Freiburg pulled one back (with a little help from Tom Bischof and Jonas Urbig) and it was an unnecessarily nervy ending, with Urbig having to pull off another big save, before Bayern made it 3-1 in garbage time when Mio Backhaus got caught on the ball in the middle of the park.

You're tempted to give Bayern a pass given the week they had -- Vincent Kompany's health scare, post-Arsenal fatigue, no Joshua Kimmich, Luis Díaz or Aleksandar Pavlovic -- but then you remember the problem wasn't creating chances. It was finishing them and managing the game. And you would have thought that the second-stringers who did play -- from Lennart Karl to Nathaniel Brown to Bischof -- might have made more of the opportunity.

3. AS Roma fight back to snatch draw at Napoli as Sam Beukema embarrasses himself: Even with their big guns unavailable (starting keeper, captain, midfield general, and most talented player ... how's that?) this Roma side gives you the sense that anything can happen. The team showed it away to Napoli, coming back from 2-0 down with 21 minutes to go and then again from 3-2 down with seven minutes left. Roma are front-foot forward and never let their heads drop, which is a credit to manager Gian Luigi Gasperini and to the players (and, for the neutral, makes them a lot of fun to watch).

As for Napoli, Max Allegri needed a win. He got a draw instead and -- again -- a red card (maybe it's the whole taking off his jacket thing). Napoli showed baby steps of improvement -- funny how if you play your talented players (like Kevin De Bruyne, Scott McTominay and André-Frank Zambo-Anguissa together) you tend to get a little better -- but let's not kid ourselves. One goal was an overhead worldie from Zambo-Anguissa, another was McTominay firing from 30 yards out -- an ode to the improbable low-xG attempts. We do have to talk about Beukema too. In the buildup to Roma's equalizer, he threw himself to the ground clutching his tummy after Leonardo Balerdi hit his arm, miraculously got back up, ran around and then threw himself back to the ground untouched after the goal. In an era of VAR, this is an incredibly unwise thing to do (especially the way officials have been refereeing this season). He should, at a minimum, have been booked and you can only hope he gets some sort of retrospective ban. If not from the league, from Allegri.

2. Enzo Maresca is right that Manchester City's defeat at Aston Villa is not a concern: I don't know if I'd have gone as far as he did ("We deserved to win") but based on performance, he's correct. Man City hit the woodwork, created many more chances than Aston Villa did and Zion Suzuki made some huge saves. One of Villa's goals came from a horrendous Marc Guéhi blunder and on the other, Gianluigi Donnarumma should have done a lot better. It's only a concern if you think that's their level and mistakes like that are going to be par for the course with those two. I don't (and, in any case, there are alternatives to Guéhi in the squad, less so with Donnarumma).

That's not to take anything away from Unai Emery and Villa. They still ended City's unbeaten league run and they're still flying higher than anyone expected after the financially driven exodus of stars over the past few seasons. I'm also happy for Nicolas Jackson. He has made huge strides since coming to the Premier League as a raw 21-year-old, and he has been treated as little more than a pawn on a balance sheet since then.

1. Juventus win away to stave off crisis talk, but we've still got a striker problem: I'm not sure how real the rumors of Luciano Spalletti getting the sack without a win at Lecce actually were, but the three away points buy him time. Juve looked fine in the first half and suffered a bit after the break, but without the 2-0 victory they'd be in the bottom half of the table, which is just not acceptable.

The issue, though, is I'm not sure that what we saw at Lecce is something you can build on. A front two of Nick Woltemade and Randal Kolo Muani is simply not viable, partly because neither has performed particularly well (between them they managed just one shot each), and partly because if you're going to play them in a 3-5-2 like they did, it means not having wingers. And for a club that invested heavily in a bunch of wide men -- Nico Gonzalez, Edon Zhegrova, Chico Conceicao, Jeremie Boga, Kerim Alajbegovic -- that makes no sense, nor will it make sense when Kenan Yildiz returns in December. Then there's Douglas Luiz, who monstered the game. Sure, he was exceptional this weekend, but if you think that will happen on a regular basis, you need your head examined. The truth is that there's a long road back to respectability. You did what you needed to do to win, but you won't get there this way.

stories.headline: George Russell: Finishing second in F1 title race 'doesn't mean anything'
stories.summary: George Russell says finishing second in the championship would not mean anything as boss Toto Wolff hit back at suggestions that the British driver may never get another shot at the title.
stories.body:
George Russell says finishing second in the championship would not mean anything as boss Toto Wolff hit back at suggestions that the British driver may never get another shot at the title.

The 28-year-old trudged home eighth at the United States Grand Prix on Sunday, the bare minimum he needed to keep the title race mathematically alive as leader Kimi Antonelli roared to a dominant victory.

Antonelli now holds a whopping 123-point lead over his teammate, with Lewis Hamilton still just about in it a point further back. Russell also now has Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc within 10 points of him.

While the Italian is likely to be celebrating the championship in Mexico City next weekend, Russell is not driven by the fight to finish second.

"As long as we win the constructors' championship, that's the main thing," a dejected Russell said.

"Obviously I'd like to finish best of the rest but P2, P3, P5 is not champion, so it doesn't mean anything."

Antonelli was in a league of his own in Austin, romping home a huge 13.0 seconds ahead of Leclerc.

But Russell, hampered by an early five-second penalty, had no answer in the same machinery, unable to get past McLaren's Oscar Piastri to progress from eighth.

- F1 readies Antonelli's title champagne in Austin: 'The race of a champion who isn't champion yet'

- F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?

- How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at Mexico GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races

"Six good laps, 50 bad laps," Russell added. "The penalty was a bit ridiculous as well, but that's the least of my worries after such a bad weekend.

"He obviously was exceptionally competitive and there are signs that the window [of performance] is very small. I hope that's an explanation for my lack of pace today, but I need to believe in my team because it's difficult to understand when you're so far off."

Russell entered the season as heavy title favourite in the grid's dominant car but his young teammate has turned the tables and is set to storm to the title.

Former Red Bull motorsport advisor Helmut Marko told Sky Deutschland this week that he doubted Russell would ever get another shot at the championship, having been usurped as Mercedes' number one.

Team principal Wolff hit back at that assertion, saying: "I think he's [Marko] wrong on George. George has all the ability. I think the car doesn't suit him.

"I think that at the beginning of the season it's difficult to cope with a situation where you're feeling like 'this is my year to come,' and then you have this wunderkind on the other side that starts to really chip away.

"And I believe that in a new season, George, if we provide him a quick car, has absolutely what it needs to win a championship."

Wolff also believes it is down to the team to understand Russell's deficit to Antonelli, taking blame away from his driver.

"George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category. I think he merits to be put in the group of the very best ones," Wolff added.

"This year we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine.

"But when it drops out of the operational window, he struggles. He struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.

"We just have to work it out. Because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all there -- intelligence, ability, determination."

stories.headline: NBA breakout players: 30 ready for the next step (yes, even Wemby and Luka)
stories.summary: Steady starter to an All-Star lock? Top-10 talent to an MVP? Breakout seasons take many forms in the NBA. Ben Golliver identifies 30 players primed to take the next step.
stories.body:
Career progression can take many forms in the NBA: cracking the starting lineup, earning a first All-Star selection or making the leap into the MVP conversation, to name a few.

Let's survey which players are primed for breakout campaigns by first acknowledging that "breakout" can have very different meanings depending on a player's talent and experience.

The 30 players listed below are all primed to take the next step in 2026-27 and have been sorted into tiers based on their current credentials and the circumstances contributing to their projected improvement.

Jump to a tier:

Breakouts to: MVP | Superstar | All-Star | Starter

Breakout picks featuring: Recent trades | Rookies

Tier 1: First MVP?
Who makes the cut: Multitime All-Stars who could conceivably break through to their first MVP in 2026-27.

Victor Wembanyama, Spurs

Last season, Wembanyama finished third in MVP voting and led the Spurs to the Finals during his age-22 campaign, cementing his status as the NBA's top blue-chip prospect since LeBron James. After proving he could captain an elite defense and survive the Western Conference's playoff gauntlet, the French center must refine his isolation scoring game and become a more dependable closer to claim the "Best in the World" throne. Given his rapid improvement during his first three seasons, those developments feel like a matter of "when," not "if."

Luka Doncic, Lakers

The Lakers have fully recalibrated around the 27-year-old Doncic, who is perennially one of the league's top scorers and passers. Doncic has never finished higher than third in MVP voting, but his candidacy should benefit from a new-look supporting cast that's tailored to his strengths and an expected spike in usage after James' offseason departure. Doncic's health looms as a potential drawback: His best chance to win MVP relies on the Lakers finishing with 50-plus wins, a bar they won't clear if he misses significant time.

Cade Cunningham, Pistons

The low-key Cunningham might not generate as much buzz as some of his contemporaries, but he checks all the boxes for aspiring MVPs by putting up big numbers, driving wins and serving as the reliable face of a Finals contender. The 2021 No. 1 pick finished fifth in MVP voting last season after leading Detroit to 60 wins and the East's No. 1 seed. If the Pistons defy their preseason doubters and finish in the conference's top tier again, the 25-year-old Cunningham will almost certainly show up on more ballots this time around.

Anthony Edwards, Timberwolves

Similar to Wembanyama and Cunningham, Edwards is another former No. 1 pick on the ascent. The 25-year-old shooting guard hasn't yet finished in the top five for MVP voting, but he has led the Timberwolves on multiple deep postseason runs and is flanked by a potent new sidekick in LaMelo Ball. Though Edwards' advanced statistics often leave something to be desired compared to past MVP winners, he has a decent chance to win his first scoring title and arguably already leads the league in charisma.

Tyrese Maxey, 76ers

Maxey is a model of continual improvement: His scoring average increased from year to year in each of his first six seasons, and he followed his first All-Star selection in 2024 with his first All-NBA nod in 2026. Philadelphia's lightning-quick guard has mastered his scoring craft, and he's bound to get more national attention playing alongside James and Jaylen Brown on the souped-up 76ers. Though Dwyane Wade, Kyrie Irving and Anthony Davis never generated much traction as MVP candidates while playing in James' shadow, the star dynamic is different in Philadelphia given that Maxey is 25 and James is 41.

Tier 2: All-Star to superstar?

Who makes the cut: Players with at least one All-Star selection who could vault into the top-15 conversation by season's end.

Scottie Barnes, Raptors

To date, the 25-year-old Barnes hasn't really functioned as a prototypical alpha scorer or proven to be a knockdown perimeter shooter. That's OK because the Raptors' forward is a very good offensive player, an exceptional defender and a strong fit alongside Kawhi Leonard. Though Barnes' winning qualities might have been masked during Toronto's rebuilding years, they should be on full display now that the Raptors expect to make playoff progress with Leonard in the fold. His positional versatility on defense, his comfort playing on and off the ball, and his imposing physicality are rarely found in a player.

Chet Holmgren, Thunder

Now is a good time to buy low on the 24-year-old Holmgren, whose poor showing against Wembanyama's Spurs in the conference finals prompted plenty of social media criticism. The 2022 No. 2 pick is arguably the league's best rim protector other than Wembanyama, and he's a skilled complementary scorer who can finish inside over smaller defenders and step out beyond the arc to beat traditional big men with his jumper. Oklahoma City's deep bench has given Holmgren the luxury of playing under 30 minutes per game throughout his career, but he's a prime candidate to pick up the offensive slack after Jalen Williams' serious ankle injury.

Jalen Johnson, Hawks

Johnson emerged as a fantasy basketball superstar last season thanks to his eye-popping production. In reality, he still has some work to do. Though the 24-year-old forward received the keys to Atlanta's offense after Trae Young's departure, the Hawks were left scrambling for answers when he faltered during the playoffs. A little patience was in order, as Johnson barely played as a rookie and missed most of the 2024-25 season because of injury. Now, his reputation is set to soar if he can lead a deep and talented Hawks team on a real playoff run.

Tier 3: Standout to All-Star?
Who makes the cut: Big names aspiring for their first All-Star selection.

Cooper Flagg, Mavericks

All signs point up for the 2026 Rookie of the Year, back for his second season with a new coach in Dusty May and a healthy co-star in Irving. Flagg, 19, led Dallas in points, rebounds, assists and steals last season, flashing future MVP potential despite his team's struggles. With James and Leonard joining Eastern Conference teams this summer, a spot could open for Flagg in the Western Conference All-Star selection process. Of course, that's assuming the shoulder injury he suffered Friday doesn't linger.

Austin Reaves, Lakers

After going undrafted in 2021, Reaves cashed in on years of steady, purposeful development by signing a four-year, $180 million extension this summer. Reaves has become everything the Lakers could want in a No. 2 option: He can create shots off the dribble, get to the free throw line, score effectively when off the ball and pass well enough to function as a lead or secondary playmaker. And the 28-year-old also has a knack for establishing strong interpersonal relationships with stars such as James and Doncic.

Amen Thompson, Rockets

Thompson, 23, was thrown into playmaking duties last season as Houston sought to cope with veteran guard Fred VanVleet's knee injury. Though Thompson responded with a productive campaign that netted him a five-year, $208 million contract extension, he appears set up for a more efficient and stable role now that VanVleet's back in the lineup as an organizer. Whether or not Thompson ever develops a reliable 3-point shot, he has All-Star tools thanks to his elite quickness, strength, power and agility. The 6-7 forward's ability to get into the paint, finish at the rim and function as a secondary distributor separates him from the average defensive specialist.

Stephon Castle, Spurs

Castle, 21, has probably supplanted De'Aaron Fox as the most likely Spurs player besides Wembanyama to get an All-Star nod. The 2024 No. 4 pick has emerged as the best player in his draft class thanks to his relentless dribble drives and physical perimeter defense. Castle isn't a natural point guard and has struggled with turnovers, but he's well-situated in San Antonio as a secondary creator.

Dylan Harper, Spurs

Harper was so electric as a super substitute during San Antonio's 2026 Finals run that he forced his way into the Spurs' starting lineup. The 20-year-old guard is a crafty finisher with excellent body control, the ability to seamlessly change speeds and a fearlessness well beyond his years. The 2025 No. 2 pick entered the season as a popular Most Improved Player candidate, and his All-Star chances will likely be shaped by how coach Mitch Johnson manages his guard-heavy rotation.

Jaden McDaniels, Timberwolves

Though McDaniels has been a favorite of Edwards and Timberwolves fans for years, he's positioned for greater individual recognition nationally after the departures of Julius Randle and Naz Reid this summer. As part of Minnesota's brash and exciting new identity, the 26-year-old forward is a strong fit alongside Edwards and Ball. Long known for his physical and versatile defending, McDaniels has blossomed into a reliable third scorer during his seven-year tenure with the Timberwolves.

Brandon Miller, Hornets

Miller has taken the reins as Charlotte's franchise player after Ball's offseason trade. The 2023 No. 2 pick didn't quite display superstar potential during his first three seasons, but his reliable scoring and high-volume 3-point shooting earned him a five-year, $209 million extension earlier this month. The next steps for the 23-year-old forward are clear: put more pressure on the rim, regularly get to the free throw line and help with the playmaking duties in Ball's absence.

Tier 4: Second unit to starter?
Who makes the cut: Former backups looking to make an impact in the starting lineup.

Ty Jerome, Grizzlies

Jerome, a journeyman who was a finalist for 2025 Sixth Man of the Year with the Cleveland Cavaliers, was bumped up into the Grizzlies' starting lineup last season before injuries limited him to 15 games. The 29-year-old guard relished his return by scoring a career-high 45 points in Memphis' season-opening win over the Utah Jazz. His controlled, efficient scoring and 3-point range make him a capable floor general for the Grizzlies' rebuilding effort.

Naz Reid, Hornets

Reid, 27, was a perennial Sixth Man of the Year candidate for the Timberwolves, but an offseason trade to the Hornets has positioned him as a frontcourt starter and veteran leader. The undrafted big man has the chops as a scorer, rebounder and defender to handle the promotion. If things go as planned, Reid will easily average career highs in points and 3-point attempts in Charlotte's perimeter-oriented offense.

Cason Wallace, Thunder

Wallace, 22, is the Thunder's designated Luguentz Dort replacement: a relentless perimeter defender who balances OKC's starting backcourt alongside two-time MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Though Wallace doesn't have Dort's broad frame, he regularly blows up possessions with his incredible hands and on-ball instincts. To live up to his new five-year, $139 million contract, Wallace must show growth as a ballhandling threat and outside shooter.

Khaman Maluach, Suns

Maluach emerged as Phoenix's starting center for opening night after Mark Williams underwent shoulder surgery in September. The 20-year-old big man is a crucial piece for the Suns' long-term future given his 7-1 frame and potential to develop into a rim-protecting stretch 5. Whether or not Maluach maintains his starting spot, Phoenix must ensure he receives a healthy amount of playing time throughout his second season. The Duke product logged a paltry 411 minutes as a rookie, making him the only 2025 top 10 pick to play fewer than 1,200 minutes last season.

Tier 5: New team, new results?

Who makes the cut: players who found greener pastures thanks to recent trades.

Walker Kessler, Lakers

Kessler is now in center nirvana after a summer sign-and-trade sent him from the Jazz to the Lakers, and he will continue enjoying a steady stream of lobs from Doncic and Reaves. The 25-year-old Kessler should even draw consideration for USA Basketball's 2028 Olympic team due to his paint finishing and interior defensive presence.

Ivica Zubac, Pacers

After thriving as a pick-and-roll partner with James Harden on the LA Clippers in years past, Zubac should occupy a similar role on Tyrese Haliburton's Pacers. Though the 29-year-old center has never made an All-Star team, he could generate some buzz if he stacks up double-doubles in Indiana.

Darius Garland, Clippers

Garland, 26, had to keep everyone involved and defer to No. 1 option Donovan Mitchell during the latter stages of his Cavaliers tenure, but a move to the rebuilding Clippers has thrust him into a score-first role. A lack of size has held back Garland in the playoffs, but he possesses enough shot-creation ability, quickness and range to function as a three-level scorer while the Clippers wait for several key players to get healthy.

Jared McCain, Thunder

Since arriving from the 76ers in a February trade, the 22-year-old McCain has been a strong answer to the Thunder's biggest weakness in recent years: inconsistent outside shooting. When Oklahoma City's half-court offense bogs down, McCain has a knack for injecting energy and flow with his deadeye shooting. Don't be surprised if there's a Sixth Man of the Year award in his future.

Peyton Watson, Cavaliers

Watson had to leave the Nuggets for the Cavaliers in a summer sign-and-trade to secure his new four-year, $88 million contract, and the 24-year-old forward cleanly fills what was the biggest hole in Cleveland's starting lineup. Though his offensive usage could take a hit given the Cavaliers' many scoring threats, he will have every opportunity to showcase his value as a perimeter defender for a veteran team with Finals aspirations.

Zaccharie Risacher, Mavericks

Expectations should be modest for Risacher, the 2024 No. 1 pick who lasted just two seasons in Atlanta. But the 21-year-old French forward landed with a retooling Mavericks organization that's seemingly motivated to fashion him into a reliable rotation player. Risacher lacks the dynamic athleticism to be a star, but he could still enjoy a lucrative career if he can pivot into a 3-and-D contributor.

Tier 6: Impact rookies
Who makes the cut: 2026 lottery picks should be able to shine from day one.

Cameron Boozer, Grizzlies

Boozer, 19, should be thrilled he landed on a roster that boasts a solid lead guard in Jerome to run the offense and multiple traditional centers to protect the 6-10 power forward from wear and tear. As Boozer tries to lead the rebuilding Grizzlies back to respectability, he has a head start on his fellow 2026 lottery picks when it comes to role definition and roster structure. That could pay off with a Rookie of the Year award.

AJ Dybantsa, Wizards

The 19-year-old Dybantsa was selected No. 1 because he is a pro-ready scorer who can get downhill and draw contact. Though the Wizards will need to juggle some competing interests as they mesh veteran stars Anthony Davis and Trae Young with a younger core led by Dybantsa, the former BYU star has the highest ceiling of any Washington prospect since 2010 No. 1 pick John Wall.

Caleb Wilson, Bulls

Wilson, 20, looks headed for a roller coaster rookie season with the dreadful Bulls: After posting a minus-45 in his NBA debut against the Raptors, he responded with 30 points and 14 rebounds in a strong showing against the Wizards a few nights later. As a 6-10 forward who plays well above the rim on both ends and can operate as a perimeter playmaker, Wilson has a strong case as his draft class' most tantalizing prospect.

Darryn Peterson, Jazz

Peterson, 19, can ease into life as Utah's starting two guard because he's surrounded by proven scorers in Keyonte George, Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. Even so, the Jazz will want to see the second pick assert himself for stretches as an off-the-dribble creator and shotmaker. Peterson proved he could get hot in a hurry at Kansas despite an injury-plagued freshman season.

Yaxel Lendeborg, Warriors

The 24-year-old Lendeborg is older and more physically developed than the typical rookie, which is good news for the reeling Warriors. With Jimmy Butler III, Kristaps Porzingis and other key contributors out to start the season, the 6-9 Lendeborg has stepped into the starting lineup and made an immediate impact as a secondary scorer and on-ball defender. If Lendeborg sustains his production in a starting role all season, will the No. 11 pick unexpectedly beat out his teenage classmates for Rookie of the Year?

stories.headline: Alexander Volkanovski could face a new challenge after UFC 333
stories.summary: Alexander Volkanovski and Petr Yan defended titles at UFC 333, but which champion could fight in a new division?
stories.body:
While both champions who topped the UFC 333 fight card successfully defended their belts, their next moves will likely be in different directions.

Featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski needed only two rounds to put away formerly unbeaten challenger Movsar Evloev. Now, he could try his luck again in the weight class that is home to two of his three UFC losses.

Meanwhile, men's bantamweight champion Petr Yan beat Merab Dvalishvili by unanimous decision to close his trilogy with the former titleholder. Yan could follow his trilogy bout with another rematch, as two possible challengers have already faced him in the Octagon -- including one who already holds a victory over Yan.

Let's take a look at the most likely scenarios and a wild card for Volkanovski, Yan and more winners and losers on the UFC 333 main card.

Alexander Volkanovski, featherweight champion
Who should be next: Charles Oliveira

If Oliveira successfully defends the BMF title against Diego Lopes at UFC 335 in December, this is the fight to make. Both are MMA legends, and neither has shown signs of falling off. Making this fight in 2027 wouldn't feel like an attempt to squeeze name value out of two fading fighters. It would feel as if it was happening right at the right time. The BMF angle doesn't add much for me, but if the UFC is going to keep that belt going, Volkanovski is more than qualified to fight for it. It would also give Volkanovski a chance to prove himself as a lightweight title contender. He told ESPN in September he didn't love the idea of jumping the line at lightweight to fight Justin Gaethje, especially with an obvious title challenger like Arman Tsarukyan. The BMF fight would legitimize the winner as a real challenger for the 155-pound belt.

Wild card: Tsarukyan

Gaethje hasn't said whether he intends to fight again. If he does, Tsarukyan is next. Gaethje has said he's next in line, and the UFC has told Tsarukyan he is. But if Gaethje decides to walk into the sunset after that White House win in June, there'd obviously be a vacant slot. Volkanovski deserves it. Send him straight into the title shot against Tsarukyan.

Movsar Evloev, featherweight
Who should be next: Pat Sabatini

I didn't love Evloev's choice of words, of "maybe I'll try again," regarding his future as a featherweight title challenger. Perhaps chalk that up to English being his second language. Hopefully, he won't be too discouraged by his first loss coming at the hands of the greatest 145-pounder ever. Regardless of his mindset, he is undeniably in a tough spot. It took him a long time to get to the top. It's probably a safe bet it will take him a while to get back. He will be in the position of gatekeeper for a minute. There's no other way to say it. The most obvious name in that group right now is Sabatini, who is 9-2 in the UFC.

Wild card: Steve Garcia

Garcia would be the second-most obvious name in that category, coming off a loss to Diego Lopes at UFC Freedom 250 in June.

Petr Yan, men's bantamweight champion

Who should be next: Sean O'Malley

Yan vs. O'Malley is the biggest fight available. Has O'Malley really earned a title shot? Since losing to Merab Dvalishvili in 2024 and 2025, he's only 2-0 -- with a close win over Song Yadong and a knockout of Aiemann Zahabi. Those two wins don't scream title shot, to be fair. But it's also impossible to strongly argue against O'Malley. He holds a victory (albeit a controversial one) over Yan from 2022. Beyond O'Malley, Song has the strongest case for a title shot -- and O'Malley just beat him in January. Even if you thought O'Malley lost to Yan back in 2022, it was a fantastic, competitive fight. We always knew the UFC would revisit it someday. I don't see why that day wouldn't be now.

Wild card: Song

If the UFC wants to give Yan this rematch instead, I'm in favor. It makes the most sense to go with O'Malley, but as a fight fan, I like the idea of Yan vs. Song, probably because of how Song knocked out Umar Nurmagomedov with one shot in the pocket. Yan vs. O'Malley would be an interesting chess match, but Song's firepower and speed are game changers. Yan will likely face both fighters eventually. O'Malley makes more sense to come first for a variety of reasons, but the more explosive matchup for Yan might be Song.

Merab Dvalishvili, men's bantamweight
Who should be next: Umar Nurmagomedov

I wouldn't expect Dvalishvili to sit on the sideline very long. He was just forced to wait 10 months for his trilogy bout with Yan, and now he's coming off the disappointment of his second loss in a row. I imagine he'll be eager to get back in the cage. The Nurmagomedov rematch is honestly a no-brainer. There's genuine heat between them. Nurmagomedov will presumably want to return by January, before he observes the Muslim holiday of Ramadan beginning in February. Their first fight was fight of the night at UFC 311 in January 2025. Nurmagomedov broke his hand early in that bout, and Dvalishvili later revealed he fought through injuries during camp. Now, both are coming off a loss, which the UFC loves to consider in matchmaking. There's a million reasons to run this one back, and I expect the UFC to do it.

Wild card: Payton Talbott

This makes sense for obvious reasons. It's a big jump in competition for Talbott, but he has earned the right to make it. Talbott has shown the kind of potential the UFC can -- and will -- reward with shortcuts. He doesn't need to beat Nos. 5 through 10 in the divisional rankings to earn a title shot. It still feels early for Talbott to make this sort of leap, but it's also the right moment to face a former champion. If Talbott loses, it's no big deal, because, at 28 years old, he still has plenty of time. If he wins, he becomes a legitimate title contender overnight.

Aaron Pico, featherweight

Who should be next: Jean Silva

I suggested this matchup after Pico's last win over Patricio Pitbull in April, and I see no reason not to double down. On paper, it's arguably the most explosive fight in the division -- especially with Diego Lopes moving to lightweight to fight Charles Oliveira in December. Silva would be a big jump up the rankings for Pico, but honestly, it's a bigger fight for Silva than most other potential top-10 matchups. Pico has always shown unmatched potential, but has fallen victim to devastating finishes throughout his career. This potential UFC Fight Night main event would be one of the scariest fights in the division for Pico. Let's see how he handles it.

Wild card: Youssef Zalal

Zalal, 30, has had an interesting career. He signed with the UFC in 2020 with a lot of hype, then went 0-3 and was cut in 2021. He fought his way back to the promotion and won five in a row before losing to Aljamain Sterling in April. A matchup against Pico would pit two featherweights against each other who have shown immense potential but haven't fully realized it.

stories.headline: Rays looking to Junior Caminero's bat, leadership in World Series
stories.summary: Tampa Bay's 23-year-old star is adding clubhouse leader to his résumé. Can he help send the Series back to Milwaukee?
stories.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- After the Tampa Bay Rays made another uncharacteristic blunder on Saturday night to continue their strangely sloppy start to the World Series, the television broadcast caught a heated Junior Caminero yelling in Tampa Bay's dugout.

His team was playing poorly against the Milwaukee Brewers for the second straight night. The Rays were giving away outs to a team that pounces on mistakes. By the end of the sixth inning, a 4-0 first-inning Rays lead had evaporated. The frustration was mounting. Caminero felt the need to speak up.

"I was trying to help the team, trying to keep their heads up," Caminero said in Spanish. "Encouraging them."

The fiery motivation attempt did not flip the momentum. That 4-0 lead became a 5-4 defeat as the Rays fell in the series 2-0 with Game 3 scheduled for Monday night at Tropicana Field. But it was a public display of an evolution that has taken shape behind the scenes, of a budding superstar emerging as the 23-year-old leader of a club four wins from its first championship.

"Junior is a leader by example," Rays second baseman Richie Palacios said. "He mostly just goes out there and does his thing. But what's exciting is when he does open his mouth, it's always useful, and it's in the time that we need it."

It was not the first time Caminero spoke up this postseason. Earlier this month, he was the only player to address the room during a hitters' meeting ahead of the American League Championship Series. He told his teammates he believed in them. He told them it was time to show the world who they are. The message resonated.

"When he spoke in that meeting, it was a little surprising but nice because he hasn't been a vocal leader," Palacios said. "We never asked him to do that. We have other guys that do that, but it just showed his love for the game and his love to win."

The Rays went on to defeat the Cleveland Guardians in six games to reach their third Fall Classic in franchise history. While mostly a frustrating series for Caminero, he came through when it mattered most, cranking a huge two-run shot off the foul pole in Game 6 for his first career postseason home run. He followed the swing with a monumental celebration and trot around the bases that clocked in at just under 40 seconds inside a frenzied Tropicana Field.

For his coaches and peers, finding his voice in the clubhouse has marked another step in Caminero's maturation.

"That has come to me naturally, trying to talk when it comes out of my heart to help the team as much as I can," Caminero said. "Despite a lot of veterans being here, I try to be able to raise my hand and say, 'Can I talk?' And then I just share my thoughts with them."

Despite his age, teammates already consider Caminero a leader for the way he plays the game. They admire all his work behind the scenes and his every-day presence; he was one of seven major leaguers to appear in 162 games this season. He plays hard.

Producing helps. Caminero is already one of the sport's best power hitters. His total of 87 home runs the past two seasons ranks second in the majors behind only Philadelphia Phillies designated hitter Kyle Schwarber. He has unmatched bat speed, an extraordinary ability to absorb information and a knack for clutch moments. He was just 19 years old when he debuted in 2023, playing in seven games before spending most of 2024 in the minor leagues.

That winter, in the Dominican Republic Professional Baseball League, he smashed a 454-foot go-ahead home run for Leones del Escogido in Game 7 of the championship series against Tigres del Licey, his team's bitter rival. He celebrated like he would two years later in the ALCS -- by taking nearly a minute to round the bases.

Rays hitting coach Chad Mottola was alerted to the Dominican series blast by a flood of text messages. He was not surprised. He said he has never seen a hitter like Caminero in his 35 years in professional baseball. How quickly he has caught up to major league pitching. His unconventional overstride, the way his hands still go up and down as he stretches. Mottola said those are mechanics that would never be taught, but Caminero's ability to repeat them with such success convinced the Rays to let Junior be Junior.

"I always go back to the first time I saw him," Mottola said. "He got called up in Toronto -- keep in mind, he was not in major league camp so I had not seen him, I had only heard about him -- and then he took his BP in Toronto and got a standing ovation from the fans in Toronto. It's another example of something I've never seen before in baseball. You realize this is a generational talent."

The right-handed-hitting Caminero established himself last season when he belted 45 home runs with a 130 wRC+. The Rays, renting a minor league stadium in Tampa from the New York Yankees while Tropicana Field was repaired in the aftermath of Hurricane Milton, finished eight games under .500. But not all was lost. They had a franchise cornerstone.

In the Rays' return to The Trop this year, Caminero cracked 42 home runs with a 142 wRC+, tied for ninth in the majors. His batting average improved 12 points from 2025. His on-base percentage -- thanks to 38 more walks -- rose 49 points. Defensively, he improved drastically as the season progressed after an ugly start in April and May. He is expected to finish second in AL MVP voting to Houston Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez. Tampa Bay has never had a player land in the top five.

"People don't see what happens behind the scenes, how much Junior works, how much Junior wants to -- not be good, because he is good -- he wants to be big in this game," Rays bench coach Rodney Linares said in Spanish during the Rays' celebration after winning the AL pennant. "And I think he has all the ingredients to be one of the best players in the major leagues."

Those ingredients have made Caminero the type of top-tier star the Rays have rarely had on their side during their 29-year history. History suggests he won't be on their side for long. Unless MLB's economic system vastly changes in the next collective bargaining agreement, the Rays likely will be faced at some point with the determination that he is too expensive to keep. Caminero has already expressed his desire to be compensated at the level of Juan Soto or Vladimir Guerrero Jr. The Rays, whose payroll this season ranked 28th in the majors, do not engage in those markets.

For now, Caminero is under team control through the 2030 season and his teammates get to marvel at his prowess.

"You're taking BP with him and he's hitting balls 200 feet farther than anybody else," Rays infielder Ben Williamson said. "I'm going up to take my round of BP and two swings into my round, the last ball he hit finally lands. Just to see the potential that's there and how good he already is, he's just going to keep getting better. It really is special."

Caminero's batting practice shows continued in Milwaukee. On Thursday, during the Rays' workout before the start of the World Series, he blasted multiple balls off the videoboard overlooking center field. One of the missiles damaged it. On Friday, before Game 1, he walloped a ball that hit the Fox set desk at the top of the second deck in left-center field.

In Game 1 on Saturday, he crushed a 112.7-mph line drive to center field for a double. But the Rays lost that game as Caminero went 1-for-3 with a walk, and they dropped Game 2 with him going 1-for-4 with an RBI.

The Rays were uncharacteristically prone to miscues on defense and on the basepaths in both defeats. Outside of the first inning in Game 2, they tallied two runs in 17 innings. To avoid an 0-3 hole, they'll need to play cleaner baseball and generate more offense against the Brewers' stingy pitching staff. For them, it starts with a budding superstar taking the reins of a franchise deep into October.

"The way he's able to step up to this moment just turning 23, and now we're going two years into it, is different," Mottola said. "There's some guys that play 10 years that take that long to get there. He's doing all these things in the moment."

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: What to watch in Kings-Rangers, Leafs-Flames, Wings-Oilers

It's Monday, so it's a typically light night on the NHL calendar.

However, all three games are interconference matchups, meaning this is one of only two times you will see these particular teams pair off during the 2026-27 season. Cherish it!

Here's a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Los Angeles Kings at New York Rangers

7 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | NYR -142, O/U: 5.5

Artemi Panarin spent more time with the Rangers than any other club in his 12-year NHL career thus far, scoring 205 goals and 402 assists in 482 regular-season games. But, following a trade midway through last season, he's now a King. This will be his second return trip to Madison Square Garden to face his old teammates, and the last time around he had an assist and two shots on goal in a 4-1 win for Los Angeles. How does this one play out?

Toronto Maple Leafs at Calgary Flames

8:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -162, O/U: 6.5

One might be tempted to look at the relative position of these two teams in the standings and conclude that it'll be a breeze for the Leafs. But these Flames are feisty! They have won four of their past five games, including one-goal wins over the mighty Hurricanes and Wild. Devin Cooley has backstopped the past three W's and continues to build his case as the best quote in the league.

On the other side, the Leafs are coming off a thorough 7-2 victory over the Flames' Alberta neighbors in Edmonton, including another two goals for William Nylander.

Detroit Red Wings at Edmonton Oilers

9:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | EDM -185, O/U: 6.5

Speaking of the Oilers, will they have any better luck against a different Atlantic Division team in this one? Saturday's loss to Toronto was the club's first at home this season, while the Wings have just one win thus far on the road.

Edmonton's big three of Connor McDavid, Leon Draisaitl and Evan Bouchard remains among the leading scorers -- as of Monday, McDavid (33 points) is 10 up on Draisaitl in the second spot. Detroit's top scorer is Alex DeBrincat, whose 12 points has him tied for 29th.

As for recent history, these two teams split the 2025-26 season series, with the home team winning each game.

On Oct. 26, 1997, Steve Yzerman became the longest serving captain in NHL history. His 11 seasons and 12 games broke the record previously held by fellow Red Wing Alex Delvecchio.

Yzerman finished his career with 19 seasons as captain of the Wings, but he has since been eclipsed by another "lifer" captain: Sidney Crosby, who has been captain of the Pittsburgh Penguins since May 31, 2007.

stories.headline: Bafana boss Pitso Mosimane's latest South Africa squad shows favouritism fears were unfounded
stories.summary: Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.
stories.body:
When Pitso Mosimane returned as Bafana Bafana head coach, sceptics feared that his proximity to South African club football would lead to an erosion of the meritocratic culture Hugo Broos had built, but the 62-year-old's second preliminary squad suggests it has only been enhanced.

Mosimane began his tenure with Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying wins over Guinea and Eritrea and a friendly victory over Egypt. Next up is the AFCON qualifying double-header against Kenya on Nov. 13 & 17.

Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.

Chicago Fire's Mbekezeli Mbokazi has returned from injury, while Aden McCarthy, Botiumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Luke le Roux, Thalente Mbatha, Nkosikhona Radebe, Devin Titus and Thakasani Mbanjwa have also received call-ups.

For every one of these call-ups, a layman can deduce a clear possible motive. McCarthy is the most obvious among them -- he has consistently featured at centre-back for Sabah in the UEFA Champions League and performed well at the highest level.

Radiopane and Xulu are in hot scoring form domestically for Orlando Pirates and Richards Bay respectively. Titus has earned his place with a strong start to life at MAS Fes in Morocco. Mbatha is back from injury and le Roux on the books of a new club at Cercle Brugge after struggling for game time at Portsmouth.

Radebe adds a right-back option from an in-form AmaZulu side with Mamelodi Sundowns' Khuliso Mudau still on the mend from injury. Mbanjwa is rewarded for a strong start to the season in goal for Golden Arrows.

Yanela Mbuthuma and Shandre Campbell -- both of whom have experienced dips in form and fortune at club level since the last international break -- are notable absentees.

In cutting two players he had given opportunities to after they had been mostly overlooked by Broos, Mosimane suggested he is willing to operate without fear or favour.

When 'Jingles' was on the verge of being appointed, Broos was quoted as telling Het Nieuwsblad: "You know, South Africa still don't have a coach. The candidate is Pitso Mosimane, a successful South African coach.

"But they know that if he comes in, they'll go five years back in time. Club owners and agents calling coaches to influence the squad selection. I threw all of them out. If one called, I would say bluntly: 'I don't talk with agents'."

The concern over agents and owners trying their luck in influencing the Bafana head coach may have been well-founded. Broos was not the first to complain of this within the national team setup.

However, questioning if Mosimane himself was open to influence without proof he was willing to make publicly available was ill-advised. It is impossible to accurately speculate on what conversations have or have not gone on between Mosimane and club owners and agents in the two months since then, but what is clear is that his team selection has been thoroughly meritocratic.

The momentum he has garnered is reminiscent of what Broos achieved in the first six months of his tenure.

At the time, the Belgian's irreverent team selection and approach to squad culture put everybody on their toes and led to an uptick in results. After they had failed to qualify for AFCON 2021 immediately before Broos was appointed, the Belgian fell narrowly short of steering Bafana into qualification playoffs for the 2022 World Cup.

In subsequent years, he kicked on and led Bafana to third place at AFCON 2023 (held belatedly in Ivory Coast in early 2024) and the 2026 World Cup round of 32.

When discussing the most successful Bafana Bafana coaches of all-time, Broos should be placed alongside Clive Barker in the top two. However, even the brightest tacticians eventually settle on patterns in their squad selection, and towards the end of his tenure, the Belgian became more predictable in certain aspects.

There was a fairly settled back five of Ronwen Williams, Aubrey Modiba, Mbokazi, Ime Okon and Mudau, and until he switched up his attacking plan to revive the FIFA World Cup campaign, Broos was likely to start Lyle Foster upfront with Evidence Makgopa the main alternative.

In midfield, Teboho Mokoena was a near certain starter and Sphephelo Sithole the clear preferred option alongside him, although Broos occasionally tinkered with his formation and left room for the likes of Bathusi Aubaas and the late Jayden Adams in the holding role. Nkosinathi Sibisi was considered another option, occasionally stepping out from the back into midfield.

Mosimane's arrival has reopened competition for places in these positions. Brooklyn Poggenpoel is retained in the squad after impressing in midfield over the last international break.

After Mbuthuma's minutes upfront, Radiopane and Xulu have been given a chance to earn theirs. Foster has made a second successive preliminary squad, although he failed to make the final squad last time out while in the process of leaving Burnley on loan to Houston Dynamo and settling in.

Fawaaz Basadien, Olwethu Makhanya, and McCarthy are in consideration in the backline. Mudau is, however, still the likely first-choice at right-back for the time being when he returns to full fitness. Still, Mosimane has done well to identify alternatives.

Mosimane declined to get drawn into a war of words with Broos over anything not directly related to matters on the pitch and instead praised his predecessor's impressive record as Bafana head coach.

In his first stint, Mosimane may not have succeeded in the hotseat. However, early results and his approach to team selection suggest he has justified the decision of the South African Football Association (SAFA) to give him a second chance and trust him to navigate the role without fear or favour to anyone.
